title: A Leaf, a Flower, a Fruit, Water
hookLine: a brass lamp packed between the sweaters
carry: bhakti: love, not the place, makes the offering
tomorrow: can a cup of tap water hold the Ganga?

lines: A BRASS LAMP IN A DISH TOWEL.
cards: A suitcase lies open on a bed. Sweaters, a coat that's never been worn, a pressure cooker an aunt insisted on. And between the sweaters, wrapped in a dish towel, a small brass lamp and a picture of Ganesha.
The flight leaves in the morning. The lamp is going too. But can worship really travel?

teach.h: THE DIASPORA: FAR FROM THE STORIES.
teach.b: The diaspora is the word for Hindus living far from the lands where their stories happened: families with roots in South Asia, making homes in other countries. Start with a woman who lived far from everything.
In the Ramayana, Shabari is an old ascetic in the forest by Lake Pampa. Her teachers are gone, and she has waited a long time for Rama.
When he finally comes, she has no temple and no priest, only fruits she gathered in the forest. She offers them, and Rama honors her. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says why that's enough.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.
teach.b: In paraphrase: whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, I accept that offering of love.
Hindus call that love bhakti, and it's the measure. So a home can hold its own shrine, a small mandir: a shelf, a kitchen corner.
Puja, worship, can happen there with no priest, and nothing on Krishna's list has to be imported. A maple leaf, a supermarket apple, tap water in a steel cup.

Now a neighbor. In the Gospel of Mark, a poor widow puts two mites into the temple treasury, and Jesus says, in the King James words, "this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury."
Both measure a gift by the heart, not the size. An honest difference: food offered in puja comes back as prasad, shared with everyone; the widow's coins don't come back.
Both still say the small thing counts.

how: Hindu families far from India keep home shrines, a shelf or a cabinet, where they light a lamp and offer flowers, fruit or water, often each morning.

o: a gathering of Hindus each year at a holy river
Hindus living far from the lands of their stories
Hindus who return to India to live in old age

p: the love that makes the offering
a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water
two mites, more than all the rest

s: Hindu worship always needs a temple and a priest
a home shrine is enough for puja; no priest required.
in the Gita, Krishna accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with love
the measure is the love, not the price or the place.
the widow's mites and the Gita's leaf teach exactly the same thing
both measure the heart; but the Hindu offering comes back as prasad, the widow's coins don't.

games.q: a classmate whose family just moved here says they can't do puja properly without the temple back home. what does the Gita verse suggest?
o: a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, offered with love, is accepted.
they should wait until they can visit a big temple again.
only offerings brought over from India count in puja.
games.why: the verse measures the offering by devotion. a shelf and a cup of tap water can hold it.

practice: Find one small thing near you that could be offered: a glass of water, a leaf, a piece of fruit. Hold it, and smell it if you can. Nothing about it needs a temple or a plane ticket.
If you pray, you can offer it in your heart; if not, rest with the plain gift of it.

wordCard.voice: The diaspora: Hindus living far from the lands of their stories, carrying the lamp, the shelf and the leaf-and-water offering with them.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water; the opening of Gita 9.26.

carryVoice: For the road: bhakti, love, not the place, makes the offering. A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water: all of it fits in a suitcase.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda, the Shabari chapter (sarga 74 in common editions; the ascetic Shabari at Pampa offers Rama forest fruits she has gathered, and he honors her)
Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, I accept that offering of love)

sources.q: this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury

sources.ref: Mark 12:41–42 (Jesus watches the giving at the treasury; a poor widow casts in two mites)
